chapman_york.text: Chapbooks, as sold on these streets since before the Vikings ran out of patience.

rail_guard.text: York Station. The curve of the roof is famous, and it is one of the longest curved platforms in the country, so the trains seem to arrive politely round a corner.
Right, where to? We'll have you there before the tea goes cold.

c_legionette.text: A small spirit in a very old helmet stands to attention, and stands very correctly, for rather a long while. It seems to be waiting to be dismissed.

then.text: Raining? Wonderful. The Minster is very dry inside, and the tour is mostly indoors today.
Sun through the Great East Window! 311 panels lit up at once. You lucky things.
Fog round the Minster today. It looks like a ghost of itself. Please don't tell the ghost tour.

yrk_guide.text: Welcome to the Minster. The Great East Window has 311 panels and tells the story from Creation to the Apocalypse. The guide leaflet is 20 pages and the best part is the sandwiches.
There are 275 steps up the central tower. I've counted them for thirty years and they've never been the same number twice. They are, I promise you, medieval.

then.text: Viking weather! A good stiff wind. Sails up, knitted socks on, off we go.
Rain on the city walls. The Vikings didn't mind it. They had very warm socks.

yrk_viking.text: The Vikings called York 'Jorvik'. In the Coppergate dig they found a Viking sock, knitted with a single needle in a technique called nålbinding. It's a bit holey, and 1,000 years old.

York had Romans, Vikings, Normans and railway barons. If you want to know why the street names end in 'gate', the Vikings' word for street was 'gata'. A 'bar' is a gate. A 'gate' is a street. It makes sense, when it's explained twice.

then.text: Halloween special: chocolate skulls. Anatomically questionable. Delicious, though.
Guy Fawkes was a York lad, you know. We don't go on about it. Bad for business, blowing up Parliament.
Chocolate oranges. York made them famous. Tap it and unwrap it, as nobody actually says.

yrk_choc.text: York is chocolate city. Rowntree's and Terry's were both here. The KitKat came from York in 1935, and they still make them in a factory just down the road.
Terry's Chocolate Orange: tap it on the table, whack it, and the segments fall out. That's the York test. Nobody has ever failed it, but plenty have been stopped by the family.

then.text: Wet day? Come to the railway museum. Mallard never minds the weather. She's indoors.
First trains in! York station in the morning is like a big, friendly beehive.

yrk_rail.text: The National Railway Museum holds Mallard, the fastest steam locomotive in the world. In 1938 she reached 126 miles an hour, which is still the record, and the driver had a neat little bit of tweed on.
York was the railway capital of the north. Seven lines met here. Even now, you can't get anywhere in Britain without a change at York, as the saying goes.

then.text: Halloween's our Christmas. Book now: the ghosts are on double time.
Christmas ghost walk tonight. Ghosts of Christmas past, present, and the bloke who still owes me a tenner.
Autumn's ghost season. Dark by six, leaves blowing about. You hardly need the ghosts, really.
Proper ghost weather this, fog in the Shambles. Look, there's the chap with the lantern again.
Getting dark. My favourite time in York. The ghosts are just starting their shift.

yrk_ghost.text: {greeting} York is the most haunted city in Europe, they say. I say there's a ghost on every street, and a ghost tour on every corner. A hundred and fifty haunted sites. And the same chap with a lantern in all of them.
The best ghost is the one you don't see. The second best is the one with a good gift shop.

york_lamplighter.text: Evening! York still has a few gas lamps, and someone has to look after them. That's me.
The Shambles by lamplight. Lovely and quiet, apart from three ghost tours trying to out-spook each other.
Mind the cobbles, they're older than most countries. The lamps are just a bit younger.

york_night_baker.text: Starting the night shift at the bakery. Bread for the whole of the Shambles by morning.
Quiet streets, warm ovens. Best job in York. Just me and the occasional ghost.
Smell that? Fat rascals are in the oven. Come back at dawn and I might save you one.

isles_sigrid.text: {greeting} I'm Sigrid. Viking, weekends only. Every February the Jorvik Viking Festival fills York with people like me, and with people pretending not to stare.
The Vikings took York in 866 and called it Jorvik. They left you words: sky, egg, knife, window. Window is vindauga, wind-eye, a hole for the wind. They were honest about Yorkshire houses.
And every 'gate' in York, Stonegate, Micklegate, is from gata, a street. So in York a gate is a street, a bar is a gate, and a snickelway is an alley. Keep up.
